title: Arrays of strings and arrays of character pointers
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its behaviour.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: An array of character arrays stores multiple strings in separate fixed-size rows, while an array of char pointers stores addresses of character sequences. These representations have different storage and mutability properties.
understand.whyItMatters: This knowledge helps reason about C data representation, object bounds and valid memory access.
understand.analogy: Think of memory objects as labelled storage and pointers as typed references to that storage.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal pointer, lifetime and object-access rules.

explain.narrative:
An array of character arrays stores multiple strings in separate fixed-size rows, while an array of char pointers stores addresses of character sequences. These representations have different storage and mutability properties.

Check the declared types, object lifetime, valid bounds and function preconditions before using the construct. Enable compiler warnings and test edge cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: Choose the representation based on whether each string needs independent writable storage or can refer to existing character data.

practise.guidedTask: Each row has capacity for twelve characters. The array owns storage for all three rows; each row is a null-terminated string.
practise.independentTask: Draw the three rows and identify unused capacity in each row.
hints: Store and print four short labels. Explain the difference between a two-dimensional char array and an array of char pointers.
A char * pointer does not automatically allocate memory for the characters it points to.
String literals should be treated as non-modifiable; use writable arrays when editing characters.
